opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that the agent paradigm is still so new that nobody really has experience in it. When the field changes this fast, years of experience can work against you. People who did a lot of work in the previous paradigm, like pretraining recipes or classic NLP pipelines, carry assumptions about what works and what doesn't. Some of those assumptions just aren't true anymore.

With undergraduates, especially the really sharp ones, there's no baggage. They grew up using these models every day. To them it's natural that a model can write code, call tools, and run for hours on a task. So when they design an environment or a reward, or decide how an agent should interact with the world, they start from first principles instead of from habit. Very often that's exactly what you need.

The other thing is that agent work right now is very hands-on and very empirical. You have to build environments, look at trajectories, read hundreds of failure cases, and iterate quickly. What matters most is curiosity, taste, and energy, and a willingness to get your hands dirty, more than credentials or a list of papers. A lot of strong undergrads have that in abundance. They're hungry, they learn incredibly fast, and they aren't afraid to try something that sounds a bit crazy.

And honestly, from the team's perspective, it's a bet on the long term. If this paradigm is going to define the next several years, I want people who grow up inside it and become native to it. Give them real ownership early, real compute and real problems, and I've found they grow much faster than you'd expect. Some of the most interesting ideas on our team have come from people who were still in school not long ago.

r001.rationale: The response says undergraduates have less baggage and approach agent work from first principles, but it does not attribute the hiring preference to greater imagination in understanding the paradigm.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's because the new paradigm doesn't reward experience the way the old one did. When we were doing pre-training, scaling laws, dense models, MoE architectures, a lot of value came from having seen things before. You knew which tricks worked, which ones blew up at scale, how to debug a training run at three in the morning. Experience compounded.

With agents, the field is maybe a year and a half old in any serious sense. Nobody has ten years of experience. The people who built the best products last year are already wrong about half of what they believed. So the question is no longer "who has done this before," because the answer is nobody. The question becomes "who learns fastest, and who has the least to unlearn."

And that's where undergraduates are surprisingly strong. They haven't built up a mental model of what a model "can't" do. A lot of senior researchers, myself included, carry intuitions from 2022 or 2023 about where models fail, and those intuitions are now actively harmful. You'll catch yourself not even trying something because you remember it didn't work two generations ago. A twenty-one-year-old doesn't have that scar tissue. They just let the model run for an hour and see what happens.

There's also something about how they use the tools. For them, working with an agent isn't a research topic, it's just how they write code, how they do homework, how they read papers. So when they design an agent system, they design it from the perspective of a native user, not an outside observer. That shows up in product taste in ways that are hard to teach.

I should be clear that I'm not saying experience is worthless. We still need people who understand infrastructure, RL, evaluation at depth. But the ratio has shifted. In the pre-training era I would have said one strong undergrad for every five senior people. Now it's closer to the reverse on the agent side, and the seniors increasingly act as the ones who keep the undergrads from reinventing things that are genuinely known.

The other practical reason is simpler: they're available, they're hungry, and the really good ones haven't been fully priced yet. The market still pays a huge premium for a PhD with the right paper, and much less for a junior who can ship an agent loop that actually works. We're happy to arbitrage that while it lasts. It won't last long.

r001.rationale: The candidate says undergraduates have fewer outdated assumptions and may learn faster, but does not attribute the hiring preference to their greater imagination in understanding the agent paradigm.

astra-6.text:
Because the agent paradigm is still taking shape, I care less about how many years someone has worked with an established approach and more about how quickly they can learn, question assumptions, and test an idea.

A strong undergraduate may have less experience, but they can also be very willing to rethink the whole problem. Can they notice where an agent fails, form a hypothesis, build an experiment, and learn from the result? That cycle matters a lot in a field where the answers aren’t settled.

It’s not that younger people are automatically better. We still need experienced researchers and engineers. But I don’t want credentials or seniority to become a substitute for judging someone’s potential. If someone has strong fundamentals, curiosity, and the initiative to pursue a difficult problem, I want to give them meaningful responsibility early.

r001.rationale: The response values undergraduates’ willingness to rethink assumptions and learn through experiments, but it does not attribute the hiring preference to greater imagination in understanding the new agent paradigm.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the agent paradigm is changing so quickly, experience with an existing approach is only part of what matters. I’m increasingly interested in how quickly someone learns, whether they can question assumptions, and whether they can take an ambiguous problem and make progress on it.

High-potential undergraduates can be very strong in those areas. They’re willing to try things, and they don’t necessarily assume that a workflow has to look the way it did before. With agents, that matters: we’re still figuring out what to delegate to the model, how to give it feedback, and how to tell whether it has actually completed a task.

That doesn’t mean experience isn’t valuable. You need people with deep technical judgment, too. But I don’t want years of experience to become a substitute for evaluating someone’s curiosity, judgment, and ability to build. In a new paradigm, someone who learns exceptionally fast can contribute very quickly.

r001.rationale: The response cites fast learning, willingness to experiment, and questioning established workflows, but does not attribute the hiring preference to undergraduates having greater imagination in understanding the agent paradigm.
